newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour presses government on Lottery report.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour presses government on Lottery report.

text.p: The opposition Labour Party on Wednesday called on the government to tighten its controls on National Lottery operator Camelot after a report that it planned to allow foreign punters to play the numbers game.
A report in the Daily Mirror newspaper said that Camelot was examining the idea of "tagging on" other countries to the twice-a-week UK lottery and allow an overseas jackpot winner.
"If the lottery is to enjoy long-term success then it must be run in the interests of the people of Britain," shadow heritage secretary Jack Cunningham said.

"That is not going to happen if people think that the lottery is hardly ever going to be won by a British person," he added, accusing the Conservatives of "caring more for rich Camelot shareholders than ordinary punters".
The Mirror report said that Camelot had considered launching a takeover bid for pools firm Vernons, owned by Ladbroke Group Plc.
It also said there was an outline plan to link up with pay television operator BSkyB to allow people to buy tickets from home.

The report also referred to talks with Bass Plc about a possible bid to run a numbers game on machines in pubs and clubs. The Mirror said Camelot directors discussed the plans at a meeting in a London hotel last month.
Camelot did not specifically deny any of the plans but said that the leaked strategic planning document was part of the process of evaluating developments in the gaming industry.
"Very many options are considered but there is a world of difference between such brainstorming' sessions and adopting them as company policy," it said.

"It (Camelot) will not pursue plans which could damage the National Lottery. Furthermore Camelot cannot undertake any initiatives without regulatory approval and permission from other relevant government departments," it added.

Camelot is a consortium owned by Cadbury Schweppes Plc, GTECH Holdings Corp, De La Rue Plc and Racal Electronics Plc, which each have a 22.5 percent stake, and Japan's Fujitsu, which owns a 10 percent stake.

The Lottery, launched in November 1994, is regularly played by some 65 percent of adults in Britain, enticed by the prospect of becoming a millionaire overnight. A second weekly draw was launched earlier this month.
Camelot, which has a licence to run the lottery until the end of 2001, raised 1.4 billion pounds for good causes in the year to end-March 1996, its first full year of operation.
But its critics have voiced concern over its pre-tax profits -- 77.5 million pounds last year -- and the salaries it pays its top executives.
Cunningham said Labour would have a non-profit operator or attempt to put a cap on profits.
